subject: history_social
passage: In Mughal India, the right to have coins struck in one's own name was among the clearest public claims to rule, and each coin recorded the name of the ruler and the city whose mint produced it. Numismatist Imran Qadri examined coins from a provincial mint during a period when a rebellious prince challenged the emperor. Coins from that mint dated to one year carry the prince's name; coins from the same mint dated to the years just before and after carry the emperor's name. Because a prince could strike coins at a mint only if he controlled the city where it operated, Qadri's findings suggest that the prince ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was accepted as the rightful ruler throughout Mughal India for that year.
choices.B: probably held that city for a time before the emperor's forces regained it.
choices.C: persuaded the emperor's own officials to strike coins in his name as an honor.
choices.D: never controlled that city, since its mint went on using the emperor's name.

explanation.why: Coins could be struck in a ruler's name only where he controlled the mint's city. Coins from one year carry the prince's name, so he held the city then; coins from the years before and after carry the emperor's name, so the emperor held it before and again afterward. Together, the coins point to a brief period of control by the prince.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Coins from one provincial mint cannot show that the prince was accepted everywhere.
explanation.B: Correct. The switch to the prince's name and back to the emperor's fits a short period of control before the city was lost.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text presents coins as a claim to rule, not as an honor granted by the emperor's officials.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The coins from that one year carry the prince's name, which shows he did control the city then.
